This radio flash left its galaxy ten billion years ago, before Earth even existed.
It lasted milliseconds. Astronomers call it a fast radio burst: FRB 20240304B.
South Africa's MeerKAT telescope caught it. It's the most distant one ever detected.
But radio dishes can't say where a flash came from, and big ground telescopes saw nothing there.
So the team asked James Webb. It found a tiny galaxy, ten million times our Sun's mass.
Its light is stretched by the expanding universe. That stretch dates it to 10.6 billion years ago.
The galaxy is young and making stars. That fits one theory: magnetars, newborn neutron stars.
It's also a flashlight. Its radio colors arrived at different times, revealing the gas it crossed.
One millisecond of signal probes eighty percent of cosmic history.
